tagline: Across Mauna Loa's slopes, from sea level to over 4,000 feet.
intro: Highway 11 crosses Kaʻū from Mānuka State Park, where an arboretum keeps 48 species of native trees, to the main gate of Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park, rising from sea level to over 4,000 feet. The western slopes pass over relatively new lava, with broad views of the ocean. Past Kahuku the road winds into the green Waiʻōhinu Valley and down to the sea at Honuʻapo, then climbs east past the flat-topped Nīnole Hills, with long views up toward the summit of Mauna Loa.
This was sugar country. At Pāhala the last sugar mill on the island closed in 1996.

moments.title: Honuʻapo
moments.text: The name means the caught turtle, or maybe "look, a turtle", and for many years the bay below was the main harbor for shipping out Kaʻū sugar.

moments.title: Punaluʻu Beach
moments.text: Green and hawksbill turtles often bask on the black basalt sand, and the name, spring diver, recalls people diving with jugs for the cold fresh water that flows in under the surf.

moments.title: Kaʻū Desert
moments.text: Near mile marker 38 the byway guide points to a pullout for footprints left in the ash of the 1790 eruption, long credited to Keōua's warriors though people crossed here for centuries.
